entry: American television series (2004–2010). Created by Jeffrey Lieber, J. J. Abrams, and Damon Lindelof, its 121 episodes aired on ABC over six seasons. Survivors of an airline crash are stranded on a mysterious island in the South Pacific Ocean, and episodes pair island storylines with flashback and flashforward sequences. Filmed primarily in Oahu, [[Hawaii]], it was among television's most expensive series, its pilot alone costing over $14 million. The first season averaged an estimated 16 million viewers per episode. It won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Drama Series (2005).

Form of [[Gambling|gambling]] based on random drawing of numbers for prizes. Some governments outlaw lotteries, while others endorse them and run national or state lotteries. The most common regulations ban sales to minors and license ticket vendors. Keno slips from China's [[Han dynasty]], dated between 205 and 187 BC, are the first recorded signs of a lottery, and such lotteries may have helped finance the [[Great Wall of China]]. The first recorded lotteries selling tickets for cash prizes were held in the Low Countries in the 15th century, when towns used them to raise money for fortifications and the poor. The Dutch state-owned Staatsloterij, dating from 1726, is the oldest running lottery. By the beginning of the 20th century, most forms of gambling, including lotteries, were illegal in the [[United States]] and most of Europe, a ban that lasted until after World War II.

American actor and retired [[Bodybuilding|bodybuilder]]. He won the IFBB Mr. America title and two consecutive IFBB Mr. Universe titles, and appeared in the documentary film *Pumping Iron* (1977). Early in his career he trained with [[Arnold Schwarzenegger]]. He is best known for the title role in the CBS series *The Incredible Hulk* (1977–1982), and he has voiced the character in later animated and computer-generated versions. His films include *Hercules* (1983) and *Sinbad of the Seven Seas* (1989), and he appeared as himself in the sitcom *The King of Queens*.

American baseball first baseman. Nicknamed the "Iron Horse," he played 17 seasons for the [[New York Yankees]], won the Triple Crown, and was twice named American League Most Valuable Player. He set a record of 2,130 consecutive games played, which stood until Cal Ripken Jr. surpassed it in 1995. His streak ended in May 1939 when an undiagnosed ailment, later identified as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis ([[ALS]]), hampered his play. He retired that year, and on July 4, 1939, at Yankee Stadium, he called himself the "luckiest man on the face of the earth." He was elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1939.

American rock musician and poet. He was the guitarist, lead singer, and principal songwriter for the [[The Velvet Underground|Velvet Underground]], a commercially unsuccessful band later regarded as one of the most influential in alternative rock. He launched a solo career after leaving in 1970. His album *Transformer* (1972), produced by [[David Bowie]], brought mainstream recognition and includes "Walk on the Wild Side," his most successful single. He reached a critical and commercial peak with *New York* (1989). He was inducted into the [[Rock and Roll Hall of Fame]] as a Velvet Underground member in 1996 and as a solo artist in 2015.

Electroacoustic transducer converting an electrical audio signal into sound. A loudspeaker system combines one or more drivers, an enclosure, and electrical connections. The dynamic driver, the most common type, shares the basic configuration of a [[Microphone|microphone]] but operates in reverse. Current from the signal passes through a voice coil in a magnetic field, and the resulting movement, due to [[Faraday's law of induction]], drives a diaphragm that moves air. The dynamic speaker was invented in 1925 by Edward W. Kellogg and Chester W. Rice. Most high-fidelity systems use separate drivers: tweeters for high frequencies, mid-range drivers for middle frequencies, and woofers for low frequencies, with a crossover network directing each part of the signal. Smaller speakers appear in radios, televisions, [[Personal computer|personal computers]], and headphones, while larger systems serve home stereos, electronic musical instruments, and public address systems.

Swiss-born American biologist and geologist. Known for observational data gathering and analysis, he made institutional and scientific contributions to zoology and [[Geology|geology]], producing multivolume research books running to thousands of pages. He studied with [[Georges Cuvier]] and [[Alexander von Humboldt]] in Paris and was appointed professor of natural history at the University of Neuchâtel in November 1832. He emigrated to the United States in 1847 and became professor of zoology and geology at [[Harvard University]], where he founded the Museum of Comparative Zoology. His contributions to ichthyological classification include extinct species such as [[Megalodon|megalodon]], and he is credited with founding glaciology. His theories of human, animal, and plant polygenism have been criticized as implicitly supporting scientific racism.

Canadian-American film producer and co-founder of [[Metro-Goldwyn-Mayer]]. Under his management, the studio became the most prestigious in Hollywood, accumulating the largest concentration of leading writers, directors, and stars. He was born in Minsk or Dymer, then both in the [[Russian Empire]], and grew up poor in Saint John, New Brunswick, where he quit school at 12 to support his family. He ran the business side, setting budgets and approving productions, while producer [[Irving Thalberg]] supervised all output. He was criticized for his treatment of performers, such as [[Judy Garland]], whom he forced to diet, take drugs, and work punishing schedules. He was forced out as vice president in 1951 when the parent company, Loew's, Inc., sought to improve declining profits. A staunch conservative, he once chaired the California Republican Party, and in 1927 he was one of the founders of the organization that presents the [[Academy Awards]].

French educator and inventor of [[Braille|braille]]. Injured in one eye by an awl at age three, he was totally blind by age five after an infection spread to both eyes. He attended the Royal Institute for Blind Youth in Paris from 1819, and, inspired by Charles Barbier's system, he developed a more compact code of raised dots that he first presented to his peers in 1825, at age fifteen. The system allowed reading and writing of letters, numbers, and music. He taught at the Institute as an adult and spent much of his life refining it. Most educators did not use it for many years after his death, but it was officially adopted at the Institute in 1854 and is now used worldwide.

American [[Stand-up comedy|stand-up]] comedian, actor, and filmmaker. He began his career in the 1990s writing for comedians including [[David Letterman]], [[Conan O'Brien]], [[Chris Rock]], and [[Saturday Night Live]]. He created, directed, and starred in the FX series *Louie* (2010–2015), which won him two Primetime Emmy Awards for Outstanding Writing in a Comedy Series. In 2017 he admitted to several incidents of sexual misconduct after an article in [[The New York Times]], and his film *I Love You, Daddy* was pulled from distribution. He returned to stand-up in 2018, and *Sincerely Louis C.K.* (2020) won a Grammy Award for Best Comedy Album.

French scientist, artist, and photographer. He invented the diorama, which opened in Paris in July 1822, and was also an accomplished painter and scenic designer. In 1829 he partnered with [[Nicéphore Niépce]], who had made the oldest surviving camera photograph. After Niépce's death in 1833, Daguerre developed the [[Daguerreotype|daguerreotype]] process, in which a silver-plated copper sheet sensitized with iodine vapor was exposed in a camera and then developed with [[Mercury (element)|mercury]] vapor. On August 19, 1839, the French government presented the process as a gift "free to the world," in exchange for lifetime pensions for Daguerre and Niépce's son. Daguerreotypes were used primarily for portraits.

American religious leader. He officially adopted the name [[Nation of Islam]] in 1981, reviving the group, a movement combining black nationalism with Islamic terminology. Before joining, he was a violinist and calypso singer, and in the 1950s he served as a minister under [[Elijah Muhammad]] in Boston and Harlem. He led the Million Man March in Washington, D.C., in October 1995. Many of his statements have been condemned as antisemitic, homophobic, or racist; he has denied being antisemitic, racist, sexist, or anti-gay. He was banned from [[Facebook]] in 2019.

King of France from 1226 to 1270, also known as Saint Louis. Crowned at Reims at age 12, he was the sole French king canonized by the [[Catholic Church]], and he is regarded as the most distinguished of the Direct Capetians. He abolished trial by ordeal, incorporated the presumption of innocence into criminal proceedings, and created a royal justice mechanism allowing petitioners to appeal judgments directly to the monarch. He led the Seventh and Eighth Crusades. He was captured and ransomed in Egypt during the first, and died of [[Dysentery|dysentery]] during the second. His treatment of Jews included ordering them to wear a yellow badge and the burning of the Talmud. His son Philip III succeeded him.

King of Hungary and Croatia from 1342 to 1382, and of [[Poland]] from 1370, known as Louis the Great. He inherited a centralized kingdom and a rich treasury from his father, Charles I. After his brother Andrew was assassinated in 1345, he accused Queen Joanna I of Naples of the murder and launched two campaigns to the Kingdom of Naples between 1347 and 1350, withdrawing in 1351. He forced the [[Republic of Venice]] to renounce the Dalmatian towns in 1358, and he waged wars against the Lithuanians, Serbia, and the [[Golden Horde]]. He established a university in Pécs in 1367, which closed within two decades for lack of revenue. Hungarian historians long regarded him as ruler of an empire "whose shores were washed by three seas."

Estonian-born American architect. His family emigrated from the [[Russian Empire]] to the United States in 1906, and he settled in Philadelphia, where he founded his own practice in 1935. He taught at [[Yale University]] from 1947 to 1957 and at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] from 1957 until his death. His style was monumental and monolithic, with heavy buildings that do not hide their weight, materials, or assembly. His works include the Kimbell Art Museum in [[Fort Worth, Texas]] (1972), and his National Assembly Building in [[Dhaka]] was unfinished at his death. He was awarded the Gold Medals of the American Institute of Architects and the Royal Institute of British Architects.

King of the French from 1830 to 1848, nicknamed the Citizen King. He was the penultimate French monarch and the only one from the Orléans branch of the [[House of Bourbon|Bourbon]] family. As a commander in the [[French Revolutionary Wars]], he broke with the republic over its decision to execute [[Louis XVI]] and fled to Switzerland in 1793, while his father was executed during the [[Reign of Terror]]. He was proclaimed king after the [[July Revolution]] forced Charles X to abdicate in 1830. He sponsored colonial expansion, notably the French conquest of Algeria, and promoted friendship with the United Kingdom. Economic decline in 1847 eroded his popularity, and he abdicated during the French Revolution of 1848, which led to the French Second Republic. He spent the rest of his life in exile in the United Kingdom.

Canadian politician and Métis leader, a founder of [[Manitoba]]. The provisional government he established during the Red River Resistance of 1869–1870 negotiated the terms on which Manitoba joined Canadian Confederation. During that resistance, Riel had Thomas Scott, a Canadian nationalist, executed, and he fled to the United States. In exile he came to believe he was a divinely chosen leader and prophet. In 1885 he led the North-West Rebellion in Saskatchewan against government forces, a rebellion that ended in defeat at the Battle of Batoche. He was convicted of high treason and executed by [[Hanging|hanging]] in Regina. His execution polarized the country along ethno-religious lines and left lasting alienation among Francophones. His reputation remains divided between a dangerous religious fanatic and a charismatic leader defending the Métis from federal encroachment.

American architect of the Chicago School, called the "father of [[Skyscraper|skyscrapers]]." He mentored [[Frank Lloyd Wright]] and inspired the Prairie School. The phrase "form follows function" is attributed to him. With Dankmar Adler, he designed many theaters and the 1889 Auditorium Building in Chicago, which included a 4,200-seat theater, a hotel, and an office tower. The firm's office buildings included the 1891 Wainwright Building in [[St. Louis]] and the Guaranty Building in [[Buffalo, New York]]. Sullivan is one of the "recognized trinity of American architecture," with Wright and Henry Hobson Richardson. In 1944 he became the second architect to receive the American Institute of Architects Gold Medal posthumously.

British and American journalist and documentarian. He wrote for *Spy* and presented offbeat segments on Michael Moore's *TV Nation*. He is known for documentaries with the [[BBC]], beginning with *Louis Theroux's Weird Weekends* (1998–2000) and followed by *When Louis Met...* (2000–2002). His studies of unusual and taboo subcultures, crime, the justice system, and celebrities are mostly set in the United States. He has received three British Academy Television Awards and a Royal Television Society Television Award. *The New Yorker* described his work as "a piercingly humane, slyly funny guide through the funkier passages of American culture."

King of France from 1610 to 1643 and of Navarre from 1610 to 1620. He succeeded his father, [[Henry IV of France|Henry IV]], shortly before his ninth birthday. After exiling his mother, Marie de' Medici, in 1617, he governed with chief ministers, first the duc de Luynes and then [[Cardinal Richelieu]]. Together they established the Académie française and ended the revolt of the French nobility, systematically destroying the castles of defiant lords. By the end of the 1620s, Richelieu had made "the royal monopoly of force" the ruling doctrine. The reign also involved struggles against the [[Huguenots]] and Habsburg [[Spain]].

King of France from 1643 to 1715, known as the Sun King. He is the longest-reigning monarch in history, with 72 years and 110 days on the throne, and his reign brought a golden age of French culture and an expansion of the [[French colonial empire]]. As an absolute monarch, he diminished the power of the nobility and ruled from the [[Palace of Versailles]], where many nobles were compelled to reside. His revocation of the Edict of Nantes abolished the rights of the [[Huguenots]] and effectively forced many to emigrate or convert. France fought the Franco-Dutch War, the Nine Years' War, and the [[War of the Spanish Succession]] during his personal rule. He patronized artists including [[Molière]], and his achievements include the founding of the French Academy of Sciences.

King of France from 1461 to 1483, called the Prudent. He rebelled against his father, Charles VII, in the Praguerie of 1440, and later fled to the court of [[Duchy of Burgundy|Burgundy]]. His intrigues earned him the nicknames "the Cunning" and "the Universal Spider." By the Treaty of Picquigny (1475) with [[Edward IV]] of England, he isolated Charles the Bold from his English allies and formally ended the [[Hundred Years' War]]. After Charles the Bold died at the Battle of Nancy in 1477, the dynasty of the dukes of Burgundy ended, and Louis seized Burgundian territories, including Burgundy itself and Picardy. He eliminated rebellious vassals and expanded royal power before dying, leaving his only surviving son, Charles VIII, as successor.

King of France from 1814 to 1824, except for the [[Hundred Days]] in 1815, known as the Desired. Brother of [[Louis XVI]], he held the title Count of Provence and spent 23 years in exile during the French Revolution and Napoleonic era. His Bourbon Restoration government was a constitutional monarchy under the Charter of 1814, which substantially reduced royal prerogative. His return in 1815 led to a second wave of White Terror. He was the last king or emperor of France to die reigning.

King of France from 1774 to 1792, the last before the fall of the monarchy. His early reforms, inspired by Enlightenment ideas, were blocked by the nobility. Deregulation of the grain market raised bread prices, and in 1775 scarcity provoked revolt. From 1776 he supported the North American colonists against Great Britain, a policy that added to the debt and financial crisis and led to the convening of the Estates General of 1789. Discontent with the absolute monarchy, personified by the king and his wife, [[Marie Antoinette]], intensified into revolution. After his unsuccessful flight to Varennes in 1791, the monarchy was abolished, and he was tried for high treason by the National Convention and executed by [[Guillotine|guillotine]].

King of France from 1715 to 1774, known as Louis the Beloved. He succeeded his great-grandfather [[Louis XIV]] at age five, and Philippe II, Duke of Orléans, governed as regent until 1723. Cardinal Fleury was chief minister from 1726 until 1743. In 1748 he returned the Austrian Netherlands, and after the [[Seven Years' War]] he ceded [[New France]] to Great Britain and Spain in 1763. He incorporated the Duchy of Lorraine and the Corsican Republic into France. Historians generally criticize his reign for weakening France, depleting the treasury, and discrediting the absolute monarchy, though a minority of scholars argue that his reputation was blackened by later revolutionary propaganda. His grandson [[Louis XVI]] inherited a kingdom on the brink of financial disaster.
